Pref. Julian] Modelled on S. himself. The name may suggest treachery (because of the Roman
Emperor, Julian the Apostate) and may have been suggested by the Julian Alps, visible from Venice and
mentioned by S. in the letter describing his meeting with Byron (L ii 37). S. may also have had in mind
‘Count Julian . . . a powerful Lord among the Wisi-Goths, now a renegade’ from Southey’s epic, Roderick,
the Last of the Goths (1814). Scott in The Vision of Don Roderick (1811) and Walter Savage Landor in
Count Julian: A Tragedy (1812) wrote versions of the same story in which Julian betrays his country to
the Saracens because his daughter was seduced by Roderick, Julian’s King. Arguably, S.’s character sim-
ilarly puts private interest before the general good when he blithely fails to be of any substantial help to
